title_en: Apec summit live: Xi and Putin speak as world leaders gather in China
excerpt_en: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin
body_en: We’re back for day two of the Apec CEO Summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen. Today the summit will be addressed by APEC leaders, with President Xi Jinping set to give a keynote speech.

Bilateral meetings will continue on the sidelines, although the most eye-catching – Xi and Donald Trump, and the US-China-Russia trilateral – won’t be until Thursday. Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen this morning, greeted by a red carpet, soldiers and pom pom-waving dancers dressed in fuchsia and blue. Communist party politburo member Cai Qi, often described as Xi’s right-hand man, was there to meet him.

Trump will leave Manila, where he has been attending the Asean forum, later on Wednesday. The Associated Press reports that he has expressed excitement about his own welcome ceremony: “I hear we’re going to have quite a landing,” he told reporters. “It’s going to be a beautiful thing.”
Aside from the high-level hobnobbing, delegates are “working around the clock” to agree on a joint statement for Thursday, a senior Apec official told Reuters on Tuesday.
Carlos Kuriyama, director of the Apec policy support unit, said all 21 Apec members agreed on the need to ensure trade is “not only open, but also fair”.
He said they were also discussing the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence.
They are working very hard to make sure that we can have a common language.”

Apec opens in China's tech hub Shenzen It’s been a big week already for diplomatic summits, with the most anticipated among them, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leader’s meeting, starting today in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzen.
Some observers have noted that we could be about to witness a Yalta 2.0, a reference to a major 1945 wartime conference attended by Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.

That’s because the leaders of the US, China and Russia – namely Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin – will meet for trilateral talks at the summit to discuss the wars in Iran and Ukraine, denuclearisation, economics, tech and trade.
Trump has also floated the possibility of meeting North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term.
Here is a quick recap of the latest before the event kicks off:

China’s foreign ministry said the leaders “will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”. The ministry added that: “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate. ” But it has dismissed comparisons with the 1945 Yalta meeting saying they were just “games of political scientists”.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

title_en: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link
excerpt_en: Voice, physical touch and face-to-face interactions make people more trusting, compliant and willing to share sensitive information.
body_en: Huang is hardly the first powerful person to lower their defenses. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked.

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “ human factor is truly security’s weakest link.”

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.
These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.

The comfort of a human voice Mitnick has been called “ the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.
He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.
In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.
When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.
The Midas touch Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking.

In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.
The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

A reassuring touch can make people more generous and more willing to take risks. abezikus/iStock via Getty Images The power of face-to-face Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

title_en: Fighting in Yemen has made crossing the Bab el-Mandeb even more dangerous – jeopardizing aid and refuge for millions
excerpt_en: Escalating violence in the Horn of Africa and Yemen puts greater pressure on this key humanitarian corridor.
body_en: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa.

The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region.
However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor.

Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution.
Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait.

Our years of research and forthcoming book “ Refugees Without Refuge ” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.

A corridor for travel, trade and escape Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters.

For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents.
Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence.
Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours.

Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls.

The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas.

Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate.

A lifeline for those escaping conflict Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade.

The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers.

The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti.

Members of the Djiboutian coast guard inspect boats seized from ‘delalas’ attempting to transport migrants to Yemen on April 12, 2026. Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait.
As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad.

A humanitarian corridor Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel.

UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño.

title_en: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
excerpt_en: The post They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: An aerial view of the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in September Jae C. Hong/AP Photo A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found.

A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided.
Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters.

Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph.

Guests ride the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California, in 2023. Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades.

A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety.

But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents.

“How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.”

CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle.

Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”

Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said.

When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.”
Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain.

The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel.

That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4.

Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later.

title_en: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn
excerpt_en: Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050
body_en: Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.

The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.
In a letter published on Wednesday, the CCC said the UK is “likely to miss” its climate targets if it confirms plans to allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans in the next four years.
Those changes could result in an extra 8.4m tonnes of CO 2 pollution a year from the UK by next decade.
Related: EV charger rollout in UK slows amid political uncertainty and rise in installation costs

The electric vehicle rules are the single biggest contributor to those climate goals, meaning the government will have to find other major carbon emission reductions, unless it amends the budgets to allow more pollution.
Carmakers must sell a bigger proportion of electric cars each year under the rules, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, or face fines of £12,000 per vehicle.

However, the industry has lobbied intensively for months to cut the headline targets from 80% electric by 2030 to as low as 50% or 60%, arguing that the mandate was putting them under too much financial pressure.

Electric cars were 26.6% of UK new car sales during the first 10 months of 2026, well below the 33% headline target. However, carmakers are expected to comply with the mandate using a series of loopholes known as “flexibilities”.
The committee’s chair, Nigel Topping, wrote to Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, to oppose any reduction of the targets.

Such cuts would, he said, “put the government’s commitment to tackling climate change at risk, miss an opportunity to reduce costs for a typical household by about £800 a year, increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets by up to 15m barrels of oil a year in 2030, and damage long-term competitiveness as our main export markets rapidly transition to electric vehicles”.
Some in government have become alarmed in recent months about the impact the government’s various changes could have on the UK’s ability to meet its climate commitments.

The government has just cut funding for installing heat pumps, the second-biggest decarbonisation policy. Burnham has also alienated some Labour MPs by waving through gas extraction from the Jackdaw gasfield, and considering approval for the massive Rosebank oilfield.
MPs voted earlier this year to approve a new set of carbon reductions for the years 2038-42.

However, the Guardian has learned that one cabinet minister in the Keir Starmer government wanted the government to go back to parliament to scrap those planned reductions and enact a more conservative target instead.
The idea did not come to fruition though, with other cabinet ministers mostly opposed.

An industry source with knowledge of discussions in government said that serious consideration was still being given to changing the carbon budgets in the run-up to the UN’s Cop31 climate conference, subject to parliamentary approval.
The source said it was not clear if the proposal was still being discussed. A government source strongly denied that it was under consideration.
The changes to the mandate also mean the UK is unlikely to meet the carbon budget covering 2033 to 2037.

Several analysts said the government will struggle to find emissions reductions elsewhere, given the scale of pollution from petrol and diesel cars and vans. The policy could also face opposition from the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each of which have their own carbon budgets.
Burnham on Thursday told Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, that he was “proud to support this Cop’s focus on electrification” and urged people to choose electric cars and heat pumps.
Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace UK, said: “The Burnham government cannot talk of climate leadership on the international stage while doing a U-turn on ZEV targets at home.”

title_en: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
excerpt_en: As landscapes change around us, novels and non-fiction books remain the same.
body_en: Pavel L Photo and Video/Shutterstock On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.
While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it.
Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres.

And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged.

Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels.
When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change.
Leer más: Three things historical literature can teach us about the climate crisis

Reading from the future The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work.

In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea.

The Thwaites glacier, in the eastern Antarctic, is shrinking fast, and is losing significant amounts of ice. NASA/James Yungel, CC BY-SA Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future.

An unexpected atlas Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way.

In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it?
Leer más: The Antarctic ice sheet is melting. And this is bad news for humanity
Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change.

Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them.

title_en: David Jones: what went wrong and what happens next? Five takeaways from first creditors meeting
excerpt_en: Upmarket retailer, which recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, has total debt over $400m including $11m owed to staff
body_en: Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong.
Related: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?

How much is owed? David Jones collapsed early this month owing in excess of $400m to an assortment of creditors, including $180m of debts to trade creditors, mainly consisting of the brands that stocked its shelves.
There are also outstanding employee entitlements, such as annual and long-service leave, worth about $11m, and about $33m in unredeemed gift cards, which the retailer is still accepting.

The rest is owed to large secured creditors, led by the retailer’s main financier, Hilco, which has a controlling hand over the current process and even has its own representatives in the 19 stores marked for closure.
Taken together, the debts are well over $400m, but that total is almost certain to climb as landlords tally up their losses.
On top of unpaid rent up to the appointment of administrators, shopping centre owners will also claim for broken leases after the chain’s receivers moved to close half of its 38-store network.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email How much will creditors get back? What, if any, money suppliers get back hinges on whether a buyer steps in and how much they are willing to pay, or whether the chain ends up liquidated, as well as how much cash David Jones can bring in through the crucial Christmas trading period.
Because product suppliers sit near the bottom of the creditor priority list, they won’t receive any money until secured lenders and employees are paid out.
Given the size of the outstanding debts, and poor financial state of the department chain, many suppliers are bracing for a near total loss of outstanding amounts.
Shaun Fraser, a founding partner at McGrathNicol, told creditors there were “too many variables” to indicate how much, if any, suppliers would receive.
“We haven’t yet got to a point where we’re engaged enough with bidders to have a sense of what value might be there,” Fraser said.
“We haven’t reached a point in the sale process where people are talking value or price.”

How are creditors feeling? Store closures mean at least 1,689 jobs will go, plus those from brands with in-store concessions, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA) said Tuesday.

Bernie Smith, the SDA national vice-president, said staff were stressed and did not know when they would be paid their entitlements. Only 170 staff were set to be redeployed, with offers to go out by Monday, he said.
Out-of-pocket suppliers are particularly frustrated, though the modern practice of holding meetings online kept any real anger contained behind muted microphones.
There were questions over whether there had been preferential treatment to some suppliers, and if the retailer had been trading insolvent before the appointment of administrators.
McGrathNicol said it would investigate when the company might have been insolvent, and if preferential payments were made.
One brand representative said they had also repeatedly asked for stock lists and weekly sales figures without response.
What went wrong? The administrators provided updated financials at the meeting that showed the poor state of affairs at David Jones.
The 188-year-old retailer recorded a net loss of $228m in 2025-26, before losing a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.

title_en: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
excerpt_en: Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy
body_en: Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees.

Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown.
In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day.
Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday.

Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter.
“We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.”

When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”.
When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”.

Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions.

Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.”
Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”.
“While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.”

Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. The company is also facing an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China in the wake of Huang’s resignation, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.

title_en: A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere.
excerpt_en: The post A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.

Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama.

By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar.
Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison.

For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.

Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time.
And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets.

Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.
And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.

Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder.
Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two?

As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.

Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.”

The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system.

But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country.

Ana had hoped to leave the abuse behind when she was transferred out of Dublin federal prison. Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters.

“Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”

An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.”

title_en: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
excerpt_en: The post Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Demonstrators take part in a protest in May at the Utah Capitol to oppose the construction of a data center in Box Elder County. Natalie Behring/Getty Images A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.

“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.

Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.

ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.

Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.

“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.

“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan is one of a dozen Democratic members of Congress who have called for limiting data center construction on public lands following recent reporting by ProPublica. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.

Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”

Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.

Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.

The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.

Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”

title_en: Jon Stewart on Trump administration response to air travel crisis: ‘So chaotic and amateurish’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts discussed the administration’s unhelpful response to the FAA’s rare ground stop this weekend
body_en: Late-night hosts responded to the FAA’s sudden, rare ground stop as Donald Trump shirks any responsibility for the transportation crisis.

Jon Stewart Jon Stewart opened Monday’s Daily Show with a recap of the Federal Aviation Administration’s shock ground stoppage on Friday afternoon, which stranded travelers across the country and led to cascading delays. Stewart had particular ire for the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, who comforted worried travelers on Friday evening with: “This isn’t another 9/11.”
“Who said 9/11! Why would you bring up 9/11?!” Stewart marveled. “These motherfuckers just want to know if they’re going to miss their connecting flights!”

Later in his press conference, as the crisis was still unfolding, Mullin took the time to correct a reporter who asked if the stoppage was related to an AI error – “We call it SI [super intelligence] around here, remember?” he said.
Related: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump accusing Democrats of wrongdoing: ‘His mantra is corruption’
“That’s your problem?” Stewart mocked. “Deadnaming the robots? You just invoked 9/11, and now you’re the grammar police? ‘Uh, excuse me, miss, the planes will be crashing into the Gulf of America.’
“This is so chaotic and amateurish – which makes sense,” he added. As Mullin said, “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like.”

And “while it may feel like all of our nation’s critical systems are falling apart, each one on a different day, like an advent calendar of societal collapse, help is on the way,” Stewart added, referring to the rumored comeback of the disgraced Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, following his affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

“A comeback? Oh, it’s been a long weekend,” Stewart quipped. “What’d you do, one day of soul-searching per affair? A comeback? How is this even possible?” Stewart then cut to a clip of Trump saying that he “would not mind” Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia because “he’s a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people.”

“The entire Jensen Huang soap opera exposes how all of these tech titans have us normies by the short and curlies,” said Stewart. “Like they’re creating the most powerful technology that the world has ever seen. Even they say in their filing to go public could pose an existential threat to humanity, but we are not even allowed to regulate them.”

Jimmy Kimmel “Sometimes it feels like maybe Elon and his Doge bros shouldn’t have fired more than a thousand employees at the FAA,” said Jimmy Kimmel on Monday evening, as US air travel still faced numerous delays and cancellations.

“We learned this weekend a very valuable lesson: we learned what happens when the only experience your secretary of transportation has when it comes to transportation is being on Road Rules All Stars on MTV.

“And where, you may ask, was the president during all of this?” Kimmel continued. “He was in the Oval Office meeting with his 87-year-old ambassador to Hollywood, Jon Voight. Trump pulled a real disappearing act on this one. He didn’t post about it Friday or Saturday. But he did find time to complain about the public golf course he’s trying to forcibly renovate in Washington.”

That would be the city’s East Potomac Park and Golf Link, which Trump calls “Trash Island”. Trump wrote on Truth Social: “Trash Island is currently the worst golf course anywhere in the world. The fairways are far too close together. When you walk down the corridors of Trash Island, you don’t hear the sound of the running Potomac. All you hear is the sound of people screaming, ‘FORE!’”

“You might be wondering, with all that’s going on, why the president is posting about ‘Trash Island’,” Kimmel noted. “It’s very simple: Now that he can’t go to Epstein’s island, you know, he needs an island. He needs one island at all times.”
Seth Meyers And on Late Night, Seth Meyers skewered Trump’s refusal to engage with the FAA stoppage on any level. As Trump told the press on Monday: “I don’t take any responsibility.”
“No, of course not! Why would you?” Meyers retorted. “The constitution says the president’s only responsibilities are tweets, memes and ballrooms.

“After several days of near silence, the president finally emerged from hiding to explain to a worried nation that the air traffic control system, the one that keeps us all safe while flying, had a heart attack and that’s why he wants to blow it up,” said Meyers of Trump’s eventual comments on the matter to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House. “Is there anything else you’d like to explain to the class before we go to the school board and demand to have you removed?”

Meyers then played a clip of Trump claiming that “the Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass” for the nation’s flight communication system, which was not advised “if you know anything about electrical engineering”.
“Now, if you’re wondering if you cannot hook up copper into glass, the answer is actually yes, he’s correct,” Meyers joked.

“Of course he’s not fucking right!” he added. “You can transmit data from copper to glass the same way Trump transmits data to the media from his ass. Do you seriously think the same oatmeal-brained 80-year-old who once spelled the word tap with two Ps was secretly an electrical engineer this whole time?”
